chapters.title: Tokens, Variables, Operators & Interactive Input/Output
chapters.overview: Covers the building blocks of Python programming for CBSE Class 10: character sets, tokens (keywords, identifiers, literals, operators, punctuators), variables, dynamic typing, input() and print() with sep and end parameters.

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: print() with sep & end
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax: print("CBSE", "Class", 10, sep="-", end="!\n")
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: Default sep is space " " and default end is newline "\n".

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: Numeric Input Conversion
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax: marks = float(input("Enter marks: "))
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: input() always returns a string (str); cast with int() or float() for arithmetic.

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: Floor Division & Modulo
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax:
quotient = 17 // 5   # 3
remainder = 17 % 5   # 2
power = 2 ** 4       # 16
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: // truncates toward negative infinity; % returns the remainder.

topics.title: 1.1 Python Tokens, Identifiers & Data Types
topics.summary: A token is the smallest individual unit in a Python program. Python has 5 token types: Keywords, Identifiers, Literals, Operators, and Punctuators.
keyPoints: Identifiers can contain letters (A-Z, a-z), digits (0-9), and underscores (_), but CANNOT start with a digit.
Keywords like False, None, True, def, if, elif, else, for, while, import are case-sensitive (only True, False, None are capitalized!).
Core Data Types: int, float, str, bool, list, tuple, dict, NoneType.
Use type(x) to inspect the data type and id(x) to inspect the memory address of an object.
topics.boardTip: CBSE 1-Mark Favourite: Which of the following is an invalid identifier? e.g. `my_var_1` (Valid), `_score` (Valid), `2nd_place` (Invalid — starts with digit), `my-score` (Invalid — hyphen is subtraction operator).

codeExamples.title: Interactive Student Profile & Type Inspector
codeExamples.description: Reads student details via input() and inspects Python data types.
codeExamples.code:
# CBSE Class 10 - Chapter 1: Variables, Types & Interactive input()
student_name = input("Enter Student Name: ")
roll_no = int(input("Enter Roll Number: "))
percentage = float(input("Enter Pre-Board Percentage: "))

print("\n--- CBSE Class 10 Student Summary ---")
print("Name:", student_name, "| Type:", type(student_name).__name__)
print("Roll No:", roll_no, "| Type:", type(roll_no).__name__)
print("Percentage:", percentage, "| Type:", type(percentage).__name__)
print("Status", "Passed", sep=" -> ", end=" 🌟\n")

topics.title: 1.2 Arithmetic, Relational & Logical Operators
topics.summary: Operators perform computations and comparisons. Understanding operator precedence (PEMDAS / BODMAS) is essential for CBSE output questions.
keyPoints: Exponentiation `**` has the highest arithmetic precedence and is right-associative (`2 ** 3 ** 2` = `2 ** 9` = `512`!).
`/` (True Division) ALWAYS returns a `float` (e.g., `10 / 2` gives `5.0`).
`//` (Floor Division) returns an `int` if both operands are `int`, or a `float` if either operand is `float` (`10.0 // 3` gives `3.0`).
Logical operators precedence: `not` > `and` > `or`.
topics.boardTip: Watch out for `2 ** 3 ** 2` in exams! Because `**` evaluates right-to-left, `3 ** 2` is evaluated first (`9`), giving `2 ** 9 = 512` (not `64`).

codeExamples.title: Operator Precedence & EMI/Interest Calculator
codeExamples.description: Demonstrates arithmetic operators, floor division, and right-associative exponentiation.
codeExamples.code:
# CBSE Class 10 - Operators & Precedence Demo
principal = float(input("Enter Principal Amount (₹): "))
rate = float(input("Enter Annual Rate (%): "))
time_years = int(input("Enter Time (years): "))

simple_interest = (principal * rate * time_years) / 100
compound_amount = principal * ((1 + rate / 100) ** time_years)

print(f"\nSimple Interest : ₹{simple_interest:.2f}")
print(f"Compound Amount : ₹{compound_amount:.2f}")
print("\n--- Board Exam Precedence Check ---")
print("2 ** 3 ** 2 =", 2 ** 3 ** 2, "(Right-to-left associativity)")
print("17 // 5 =", 17 // 5, "| -17 // 5 =", -17 // 5)

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: for-else / while-else
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: The else block of a loop executes ONLY if the loop finishes normally without hitting a break statement.

topics.title: 2.1 Decision Making with if, elif, else
topics.summary: Conditional statements test boolean expressions and execute indented blocks accordingly.
keyPoints: Indentation (4 spaces) defines block scope in Python.
`elif` allows testing multiple mutually exclusive conditions; as soon as one branch is True, the rest are skipped.
Nested `if` statements allow checking secondary conditions inside an outer branch.

topics.title: 2.2 Iteration: for, while, break, continue & Patterns
topics.summary: Use `for` loops when the number of iterations is known (or when traversing a sequence) and `while` loops for condition-controlled repetition.
keyPoints: `break` terminates the innermost loop immediately.
`continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next iteration.
A `for` or `while` loop can have an optional `else:` block that runs only if `break` was never triggered.
topics.boardTip: For prime number checking, using `for...else` is the cleanest Pythonic pattern: check divisors from `2` to `int(n**0.5) + 1`!

chapters.title: Strings, Lists & Tuples in Python
chapters.overview: Comprehensive guide to indexing (positive & negative), slicing, mutability vs immutability, built-in string methods, and list manipulation functions.

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: List Slicing & Reversal
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax:
items[start : stop : step]
items[::-1]  # Reverses sequence
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: Negative indices count from the right starting at -1.

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: append() vs extend()
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax:
L.append([4, 5])  # Adds as single nested list
L.extend([4, 5])  # Adds 4 and 5 individually
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: Frequently tested in CBSE 1-mark and 2-mark questions!

topics.title: 3.1 Lists: Indexing, Slicing & Built-in Methods
topics.summary: Lists are ordered, mutable sequences enclosed in square brackets `[]`. Elements can be modified in-place.
keyPoints: `L.append(x)` adds `x` at the end; `L.insert(i, x)` inserts `x` at index `i`.
`L.pop(i)` removes and returns item at index `i` (default `-1`); `L.remove(val)` deletes first occurrence of `val`.
`L.sort()` sorts the list in-place and returns `None`, whereas `sorted(L)` returns a new sorted list!
topics.boardTip: Trap Alert: `res = my_list.sort()` assigns `None` to `res` because `.sort()` modifies the list in-place!

codeExamples.title: Interactive Class Marks Analyzer using Lists

codeExamples.code:
# CBSE Class 10 - List Operations & Marks Analyzer

for i in range(1, n + 1):

topics.summary: Data Science in AI starts with summarizing numerical datasets using Mean (average), Median (middle value), and Mode (most frequent value).
keyPoints: Mean is sensitive to extreme outliers; Median is robust against outliers.
Mode can be used for both numerical and categorical data.

chapters.title: Python Revision Tour I & II (Mutability, Slicing & Dictionaries)
chapters.overview: Covers Class 11 foundations tested heavily in Class 12 Section A & B: Mutable vs Immutable objects, shallow vs deep copy, tricky string/list/tuple slicing, and dictionary methods.

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: Mutable vs Immutable Types
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax:
Immutable: int, float, bool, str, tuple
Mutable  : list, dict, set
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: Dictionary keys MUST be immutable types (str, int, or tuple without mutable elements).

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: Safe Dictionary Lookup & Update
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax:
d.get(key, default_val)
d.setdefault(key, 0)
d1.update(d2)
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: d.get("x", 0) avoids KeyError when key "x" does not exist.

topics.title: 1.1 Mutability, Aliasing vs Cloning & Tuple Unpacking
topics.summary: Assigning `B = A` on a list creates an alias (both point to the same memory id). Modifying `B` also modifies `A` unless cloned with `B = A.copy()` or `B = A[:]`.
keyPoints: Single-element tuple requires a trailing comma: `t = (10,)` is a `tuple`, whereas `t = (10)` is just an `int`!
Even though a `tuple` is immutable, if it contains a mutable `list` inside it (`t = (1, [2, 3])`), `t[1].append(4)` is valid and mutates the inner list!
`str.partition(sep)` always returns a 3-tuple `(before, sep, after)`, whereas `str.split(sep)` returns a `list` without the separator.
topics.boardTip: CBSE Board Classic: `t = (10, [20, 30])` followed by `t[1][0] = 99` does NOT raise an error because the list inside the tuple is mutable!

codeExamples.title: CBSE Board Slicing, Tuple Mutability & Dictionary Frequency Counter
codeExamples.description: Demonstrates classic Class 12 Section A/B edge cases and character frequency counting.
codeExamples.code:
# CBSE Class 12 - Revision Tour: Mutability & Dictionary Counter
text = input("Enter a word or phrase (e.g. MISSISSIPPI): ").strip() or "MISSISSIPPI"

freq = {}
for ch in text:
    freq[ch] = freq.get(ch, 0) + 1

print("\nCharacter Frequency Dictionary:", freq)

# Classic Board Exam Tuple with Mutable List Element:
record = ("Roll-101", [88, 92, 79])
record[1].append(95)
print("Updated Tuple with Inner List:", record)

# partition() vs split() comparison:
email = "student@cbse.gov.in"
print("partition('@') ->", email.partition("@"))
print("split('@')     ->", email.split("@"))

chapters.title: Working with Functions, Parameters & LEGB Variable Scope
chapters.overview: User-defined functions, positional/default/keyword arguments, returning multiple values as tuples, LEGB (Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in) scope rules, and mutable default argument traps.

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: Parameter Ordering Rule
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax:
def calc(a, b=10, c=20):  # Valid
# Non-default parameters MUST precede default parameters!
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: def calc(a=10, b) raises a SyntaxError!

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: LEGB Scope & global Keyword
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: Without `global counter`, assigning `counter += 5` inside a function raises UnboundLocalError.

topics.title: 2.1 Function Arguments, Return Values & Global Scope Tracing
topics.summary: Every CBSE Class 12 CS paper includes at least two output-tracing questions based on default parameters and `global` variable mutation.
keyPoints: If a function has no `return` statement (or just `return`), it implicitly returns `None`.
Returning multiple values `return a, b, c` packs them into a `tuple` `(a, b, c)`.

Passing a `list` to a function and calling `.append()` or index assignment `L[0] = x` modifies the caller’s list, whereas reassigning `L = [1, 2]` inside the function only rebinds the local reference!
topics.boardTip: When tracing output questions, always maintain two columns on your rough sheet: **Global X** and **Local X**!

codeExamples.title: CBSE Board Scope Tracer & Multi-Return Function
codeExamples.description: Traces global vs local variables and returns multiple statistics from a function.
codeExamples.code:
# CBSE Class 12 - Functions, Default Args & LEGB Scope
val = 50

def changer(p, q=10):
    global val
    val = val + p + q
    p = p * 2
    print(f"Inside changer -> val={val}, p={p}, q={q}")
    return val

print("Initial val:", val)
res1 = changer(15)
print("After changer(15) ->", res1)
res2 = changer(5, 25)
print("After changer(5, 25) ->", res2)

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: Full try-except-else-finally Block
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: else runs ONLY when no exception occurs in try; finally runs ALWAYS.

topics.title: 3.1 Built-in Exceptions & try-except-else-finally Flow
topics.summary: Exception handling prevents abrupt program termination when runtime errors occur.
keyPoints: `ZeroDivisionError`: division or modulo by zero.
`ValueError`: right type but inappropriate value, e.g. `int("xyz")`.
`TypeError`: operation applied to incompatible types, e.g. `"Age: " + 18`.
`EOFError`: `input()` hits end-of-file OR `pickle.load(f)` reaches the end of a binary file!
`KeyError`: missing dictionary key; `IndexError`: out-of-range sequence index.

chapters.title: File Handling — Text Files (.txt), seek() & tell()
chapters.overview: Opening and closing text files, file access modes (r, w, a, r+, w+, a+), reading methods (read, readline, readlines), writing methods (write, writelines), file pointer manipulation with seek() and tell(), and classic CBSE text file algorithms.

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: read() vs readline() vs readlines()
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax:
f.read(n)      -> returns str (up to n chars)
f.readline()   -> returns single line str
f.readlines()  -> returns list of line strings
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: Crucial return type distinction for CBSE 1-mark and 3-mark questions!

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: seek(offset, reference_point) & tell()
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax:
f.tell()       -> current byte position (int)
f.seek(0)      -> move pointer to beginning of file
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: In text mode, seek(offset, 0) from start of file is standard.

topics.title: 4.1 CBSE Board Text File Algorithms (Lines, Words & Characters)
topics.summary: Every CBSE Class 12 exam features a 3-mark function on text files: either character-level (`f.read()`), word-level (`f.read().split()`), or line-level (`for line in f:` or `f.readlines()`).
keyPoints: Use `with open("story.txt", "r") as f:` so the file closes automatically.
To count words starting with a vowel or having length < 4, use `words = f.read().split()`.
To count lines starting with `"A"` or `"T"`, iterate `for line in f:` and check `if line.lstrip().upper().startswith("A"):`.
topics.boardTip: Remember: `f.writelines(list_of_strings)` does NOT add newline `\n` characters automatically—you must include `\n` at the end of each string!

codeExamples.title: Live Runnable Text File Creator, Analyzer & seek()/tell() Demo
codeExamples.description: Creates story.txt in the sandbox and performs CBSE-style line, word, and vowel analysis.
codeExamples.code:
# CBSE Class 12 - Text File Handling (Runs live in sandbox!)
sample_lines = [
    "Artificial Intelligence is transforming education.\n",
    "Python makes file handling simple and readable.\n",
    "Always close files or use the with statement.\n",
    "All students can master Computer Science!\n"
]

# 1. Write sample lines to story.txt
with open("story.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.writelines(sample_lines)

# 2. CBSE Board Question: Count lines starting with 'A', words < 5 chars, and vowels
with open("story.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print("Initial pointer position f.tell():", f.tell())
    content = f.read()
    print("Pointer after f.read() -> f.tell():", f.tell())

    # Reset file pointer back to byte 0 using seek(0)
    f.seek(0)
    lines = f.readlines()

lines_starting_with_a = sum(1 for ln in lines if ln.strip().upper().startswith("A"))
words = content.split()
short_words = [w for w in words if len(w) <= 4]
vowels = sum(1 for ch in content.lower() if ch in "aeiou")

print("\n📄 Text File Analysis of 'story.txt':")
print(f"  • Total Lines               : {len(lines)}")
print(f"  • Lines starting with 'A'   : {lines_starting_with_a}")
print(f"  • Total Words               : {len(words)}")
print(f"  • Words with <= 4 chars     : {len(short_words)} -> {short_words}")
print(f"  • Total Vowels              : {vowels}")

chapters.title: Binary Files (pickle module) & CSV Files (csv module)
chapters.overview: Serialization and deserialization using pickle.dump() and pickle.load(), EOFError loop pattern for reading binary files, and reading/writing tabular CSV files with csv.reader() and csv.writer() using newline="".

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: Binary File Read Loop (pickle)
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: pickle.load(f) raises EOFError when no more objects remain in the binary file.

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: CSV File Open without Blank Lines
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax:
import csv
with open("data.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["Roll", "Name"])
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: Always pass newline="" in open() on Windows to prevent extra blank rows between records!

topics.title: 5.1 Binary File Operations: Append, Search & Filter with pickle
topics.summary: Binary files store Python objects (lists, dictionaries) directly in byte stream format using the `pickle` module (`wb`, `ab`, `rb`).
keyPoints: `pickle.dump(obj, file_handle)` writes a Python object to a binary file.
`pickle.load(file_handle)` reads one Python object at a time and raises `EOFError` at end of file.
Always open binary files with `"wb"`, `"ab"`, `"rb"`, or `"rb+"`.

codeExamples.title: CBSE 4-Mark Binary File (`student.dat`) Write & Search Program
codeExamples.description: Creates student.dat using pickle.dump() and searches for students scoring > 85%.
codeExamples.code:
import pickle

def create_binary_records():
    students = [
        [101, "Aarav Sharma", 92.5],
        [102, "Diya Patel", 78.0],
        [103, "Rohan Verma", 88.5],
        [104, "Meera Nair", 95.0]
    ]
    with open("student.dat", "wb") as f:
        for stu in students:
            pickle.dump(stu, f)
    print("✅ Wrote 4 records to binary file 'student.dat'.")

def search_merit_students(min_marks=85.0):
    print(f"\n🔍 Searching 'student.dat' for Marks >= {min_marks}:")
    found = 0
    with open("student.dat", "rb") as f:
        try:
            while True:
                rec = pickle.load(f)
                if rec[2] >= min_marks:
                    print(f"  • Roll: {rec[0]} | Name: {rec[1]:14} | Marks: {rec[2]}%")
                    found += 1
        except EOFError:
            pass
    print(f"Total Merit Students Found: {found}")

create_binary_records()
search_merit_students(85.0)

codeExamples.title: CBSE 4-Mark CSV File (`employees.csv`) Writer & Reader
codeExamples.description: Writes employee records using csv.writer() and filters salaries using csv.reader().
codeExamples.code:
import csv

def write_employees_csv():
    header = ["EmpID", "Name", "Department", "Salary"]
    rows = [
        ["E101", "Kabir", "AI Research", "85000"],
        ["E102", "Ananya", "Cloud Ops", "72000"],
        ["E103", "Vikram", "CyberSecurity", "94000"]
    ]
    with open("employees.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        writer = csv.writer(f)
        writer.writerow(header)
        writer.writerows(rows)
    print("✅ Created 'employees.csv' with newline=''")

def read_high_earners():
    print("\n📊 Employees earning > ₹80,000:")
    with open("employees.csv", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        reader = csv.reader(f)
        header = next(reader)  # Skip header row!
        for row in reader:
            if int(row[3]) > 80000:
                print(f"  • {row[0]} - {row[1]} ({row[2]}): ₹{row[3]}")

write_employees_csv()
read_high_earners()

chapters.title: Data Structures — Stack Implementation using Python Lists (LIFO)
chapters.overview: Guaranteed 3-to-4 mark question in CBSE Class 12 CS Paper! Covers LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) principle, Push (append), Pop (pop), Peek (stack[-1]), Overflow/Underflow conditions, and conditional push from dictionaries/lists.

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: Push, Pop & Peek on List Stack
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax:
stack.append(item)         # PUSH
if not stack: "Underflow"  # Check Empty
stack.pop()                # POP
stack[-1]                  # PEEK (Top element)
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: Always check `if len(stack) == 0:` (or `if not stack:`) before calling `stack.pop()`!

topics.title: 6.1 CBSE 3-Mark Stack Push & Pop Pattern
topics.summary: CBSE Board exams ask you to write `PushOn(stack, data)` and `PopFrom(stack)` functions that filter a dictionary or list of records and pop all items until "Stack Empty".
keyPoints: LIFO means the last element pushed onto the stack is the first element popped out.
Attempting to pop from an empty stack causes an **Underflow** condition (`IndexError: pop from empty list` if unchecked).
Top of the stack is always at index `len(stack) - 1` (or `-1`).

chapters.title: Computer Networks, Topologies, Devices, Protocols & 5-Mark Case Study
chapters.overview: Types of networks (PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN), transmission media (Twisted Pair, Coaxial, Optical Fiber, Radio/Microwave/Satellite), networking devices (Modem, RJ45, Repeater, Hub, Switch, Router, Gateway), topologies (Star, Bus, Tree), protocols, and the 5-Mark Campus Layout Case Study.

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: 5-Mark Case Study Golden Rules
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax:
1. Server Location -> Block with MAXIMUM computers (80-20 rule)
2. Cable Layout    -> Star topology from Server Block OR shortest cable distance
3. Repeater        -> Between blocks where distance > 70m to 100m
4. Switch          -> Inside EVERY block to connect computers
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: Guaranteed 5-mark Section E question in every CBSE Class 12 CS & IP Board Exam!

topics.title: 7.1 Networking Devices, Protocols & 5-Mark Case Study Solver
topics.summary: Master the exact decision rules for the 5-Mark Campus Network Design question in Section E.
keyPoints: **Switch vs Hub**: A Switch is an intelligent device that unicasts data frames only to the target MAC address; a Hub broadcasts to all ports.
**Router vs Gateway**: A Router connects networks using similar protocols and forwards packets by IP address; a Gateway connects dissimilar networks.
**Repeater**: Regenerates weakened signals when cable length exceeds ~70–100 meters.
**Protocols**: HTTP/HTTPS (Web), FTP (File Transfer), SMTP (Sending Email), POP3/IMAP (Receiving Email), VoIP (Voice calls over IP), Telnet/SSH (Remote login).

codeExamples.title: Interactive CBSE 5-Mark Network Case Study Analyzer in Python
codeExamples.description: Calculates optimal server block (80-20 rule) and repeater placement for a 4-block campus!
codeExamples.code:
# CBSE Class 12 - Interactive 5-Mark Network Case Study Solver
blocks = {
    "Admin Block": 45,
    "Finance Block": 28,
    "R&D Wing": 140,
    "HR Wing": 35
}

distances = [
    ("R&D Wing", "Admin Block", 65),
    ("R&D Wing", "Finance Block", 115),
    ("R&D Wing", "HR Wing", 85)
]

print("🏢 Campus Blocks & Computer Counts:")
for blk, count in blocks.items():
    print(f"  • {blk:15} : {count} computers")

best_server = max(blocks, key=blocks.get)
print(f"\n✅ Q1. Optimal Server Location: '{best_server}' ({blocks[best_server]} computers)")
print("   Reason: 80-20 Network Rule — reduces inter-block traffic by hosting server where most computers reside.")

print("\n✅ Q2. Repeater Placement Check (Threshold > 80 meters):")
for b1, b2, dist in distances:
    need_rep = "YES (Install Repeater)" if dist > 80 else "No repeater needed"
    print(f"  • {b1} <-> {b2} ({dist}m) : {need_rep}")

chapters.title: Relational Databases, SQL Queries, Joins & Python-SQL Connectivity
chapters.overview: Worth 20 Marks in CBSE Class 12! Covers RDBMS keys (Primary, Candidate, Alternate, Foreign), Degree vs Cardinality, DDL/DML queries, Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX), GROUP BY & HAVING, Joins, and Python database connectivity using sqlite3 / mysql.connector.

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: Degree vs Cardinality of a Table
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax:
Degree      = Number of Columns (Attributes)
Cardinality = Number of Rows (Tuples)
Cartesian Product of A(d1, c1) x B(d2, c2):
  New Degree = d1 + d2 | New Cardinality = c1 * c2
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: Asked every single year in CBSE Class 12 Theory Exam!

importantFormulasOrSyntax.label: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) & WHERE vs HAVING
importantFormulasOrSyntax.syntax:
COUNT(*)      -> Counts ALL rows including NULLs
COUNT(col)    -> Ignores NULL values in col
WHERE         -> Filters individual rows BEFORE grouping
HAVING        -> Filters groups AFTER GROUP BY (supports aggregates)
importantFormulasOrSyntax.note: Remember: `WHERE col IS NULL` (never `= NULL`)!

topics.title: 8.1 Live Python + SQL Execution using Built-in sqlite3 Engine
topics.summary: Python’s `sqlite3` follows the exact same DB-API 2.0 workflow (`connect()`, `cursor()`, `execute()`, `fetchall()`, `commit()`, `rowcount`) as `mysql.connector`—and runs live right inside our Python IDE!
keyPoints: Step 1: `con = connect(...)` establishes the database connection.
Step 2: `cur = con.cursor()` creates a cursor object to execute SQL queries.
Step 3: `cur.execute(sql, params)` runs the SQL command.
Step 4: `cur.fetchone()`, `cur.fetchmany(n)`, or `cur.fetchall()` retrieves rows from `SELECT`.
Step 5: `con.commit()` saves `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` changes permanently.

codeExamples.title: Live Runnable SQL + Python Database Lab (CREATE, INSERT, GROUP BY, JOIN)
codeExamples.description: Executes real SQL queries (GROUP BY, HAVING, Equi-Join, COUNT) inside Python and displays results!
codeExamples.code:
# CBSE Class 12 - Live SQL & Python DB-API 2.0 Execution
import sqlite3

# Connect to an in-memory relational database
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
cur = con.cursor()

# 1. DDL: Create DEPT and EMPLOYEE tables
cur.execute("CREATE TABLE DEPT (DCODE TEXT PRIMARY KEY, DNAME TEXT, CITY TEXT)")
cur.execute("""
CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    ENO INT PRIMARY KEY,
    ENAME TEXT,
    DCODE TEXT,
    SALARY INT,
    BONUS INT
)
""")

# 2. DML: Insert sample CBSE Board table rows
cur.executemany("INSERT INTO DEPT VALUES (?, ?, ?)", [
    ("D01", "AI & Data", "Bengaluru"),
    ("D02", "Cloud Infra", "Hyderabad"),
    ("D03", "CyberSec", "Delhi")
])

cur.executemany("INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [
    (101, "Aarav", "D01", 85000, 10000),
    (102, "Diya", "D02", 72000, None),
    (103, "Kabir", "D01", 92000, 15000),
    (104, "Meera", "D03", 88000, None),
    (105, "Rohan", "D01", 79000, 8000)
])
con.commit()

# 3. Query 1: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(BONUS) (Notice NULL handling!)
cur.execute("SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(BONUS), AVG(SALARY) FROM EMPLOYEE")
print("📌 Q1. COUNT(*) vs COUNT(BONUS) & AVG(SALARY):")
print("  Result ->", cur.fetchall())

# 4. Query 2: GROUP BY with HAVING
print("\n📌 Q2. Department-wise Employee Count & Max Salary (GROUP BY DCODE):")
cur.execute("SELECT DCODE, COUNT(*), MAX(SALARY) FROM EMPLOYEE GROUP BY DCODE")
for row in cur.fetchall():
    print(f"  • Dept {row[0]} : Count={row[1]}, Max Salary=₹{row[2]}")

# 5. Query 3: Equi-Join between EMPLOYEE and DEPT
print("\n📌 Q3. Equi-Join (Employee Name, Department Name, City):")
cur.execute("""
SELECT E.ENAME, D.DNAME, D.CITY, E.SALARY
FROM EMPLOYEE E, DEPT D
WHERE E.DCODE = D.DCODE AND E.SALARY >= 80000
ORDER BY E.SALARY DESC
""")
for row in cur.fetchall():
    print(f"  • {row[0]:8} | {row[1]:12} | {row[2]:10} | ₹{row[3]}")

con.close()

practicals.aim: Official CBSE Class 12 Practical Program #1: Write a Python program to read a text file line by line and display each word separated by a "#" symbol.
algorithm: Create/open the text file "notes.txt" in read mode ("r").
Iterate through each line in the file object.

Join the words using "#".join(words) and print the formatted line.
practicals.code:
# CBSE Class 12 Practical #1: Display each word separated by '#'
sample_text = """Python is an interpreted high level language
File handling is very important for CBSE Practical
Practice makes every student confident"""

practicals.title: Count the number of vowels, consonants, uppercase, and lowercase characters in a text file
practicals.aim: Official CBSE Class 12 Practical Program #2: Read a text file and display the count of vowels, consonants, uppercase, and lowercase letters.
algorithm: Open the text file in read mode ("r") and read the entire string using f.read().
Initialize counters for vowels, consonants, upper, and lower to 0.
Iterate over each character ch in content.
Check ch.isupper(), ch.islower(), and if ch.isalpha(), check membership in "aeiouAEIOU".
practicals.code:
# CBSE Class 12 Practical #2: Vowels, Consonants, Uppercase & Lowercase Counter
with open("article.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("CBSE Class 12 Computer Science Practical Exam 2026!")

vowels = consonants = upper = lower = 0

with open("article.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    data = f.read()

for ch in data:
    if ch.isalpha():
        if ch.isupper():
            upper += 1
        elif ch.islower():
            lower += 1

        if ch.lower() in "aeiou":
            vowels += 1
        else:
            consonants += 1

print("File Content :", data)
print(f"Vowels       : {vowels}")
print(f"Consonants   : {consonants}")
print(f"Uppercase    : {upper}")
print(f"Lowercase    : {lower}")
practicals.vivaTip: Always check `ch.isalpha()` before counting a character as a consonant, otherwise digits and punctuation marks would be counted as consonants!

practicals.title: Remove all the lines that contain the character "a" in a file and write it to another file
practicals.aim: Official CBSE Class 12 Practical Program #3: Filter lines containing "a" or "A" from source.txt into filtered.txt.
algorithm: Read all lines from source.txt using readlines().
Separate lines into two lists: lines without "a"/"A" (stays in source.txt) and lines with "a"/"A" (written to target.txt).
Write the respective lists to both files and display their contents.
practicals.code:
# CBSE Class 12 Practical #3: Move lines containing 'a' to another file
initial_lines = [
    "Python is awesome\n",
    "Hello World\n",
    "Code every day\n",
    "Keep smiling\n",
    "Study hard for exams\n"
]

with open("source.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.writelines(initial_lines)

keep_lines = []
moved_lines = []

with open("source.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        if "a" in line.lower():
            moved_lines.append(line)
        else:
            keep_lines.append(line)

with open("source.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.writelines(keep_lines)

with open("removed_a.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.writelines(moved_lines)

print("✅ Lines remaining in 'source.txt' (NO letter 'a'):")
print("".join(keep_lines))
print("✅ Lines written to 'removed_a.txt' (CONTAIN letter 'a'):")
print("".join(moved_lines))
practicals.expectedOutput: Remaining: Hello World, Keep smiling | Moved: Python is awesome, Code every day, Study hard for exams
practicals.vivaTip: Use `if "a" in line.lower():` so both lowercase `"a"` and uppercase `"A"` are matched.

practicals.aim: Official CBSE Class 12 Practical Program #6: Write user credentials to a CSV file and search for a user’s password by User-ID.
algorithm: Open "users.csv" in write mode with newline="" and create a csv.writer(f) object.
Write header ["UserID", "Password"] and user rows.
Open "users.csv" in read mode with csv.reader(f) and search for the requested UserID.
practicals.code:
# CBSE Class 12 Practical #5: CSV File User-ID & Password Search
import csv

users = [
    ["admin_cbse", "Board@2026"],
    ["priya_12", "Python#100"],
    ["rohan_cs", "Stack$LIFO"]
]

with open("users.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["UserID", "Password"])
    writer.writerows(users)

search_id = input("Enter UserID to find password (e.g. priya_12): ").strip()

with open("users.csv", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    next(reader)  # Skip header
    for row in reader:
        if row[0] == search_id:
            print(f"🔓 Found! Password for '{search_id}' is: {row[1]}")
            break
    else:
        print(f"❌ UserID '{search_id}' not found in users.csv.")
practicals.vivaTip: Why do we specify `newline=""` when opening a CSV file in Python on Windows? Without it, `csv.writer` writes `\r\r\n`, creating an unwanted blank line after every row.

practicals.title: Write a Python program to implement a Stack using a List (Push, Pop, Peek, Display)
practicals.aim: Official CBSE Class 12 Practical Program #7: Menu-driven Stack implementation using a Python list.
algorithm: Maintain a list `stack = []`.
Push appends an element to `stack`.
Pop checks `if not stack:` for Underflow, otherwise returns `stack.pop()`.
Display prints elements from `len(stack) - 1` down to `0` (Top to Bottom).
practicals.code:
# CBSE Class 12 Practical #6: Interactive Stack Implementation (LIFO)
stack = [10, 20, 30]

def display_stack(stk):
    if not stk:
        print("  [Stack is Empty]")
        return
    print("  TOP ->", stk[-1])
    for i in range(len(stk) - 2, -1, -1):
        print("        ", stk[i])

print("Initial Stack:")
display_stack(stack)

val = int(input("\nEnter a number to PUSH onto stack: "))
stack.append(val)
print(f"After PUSH({val}):")
display_stack(stack)

popped = stack.pop()
print(f"\nPOPPED element: {popped}")
print("Stack after POP:")
display_stack(stack)
practicals.vivaTip: What is the time complexity of `append()` (Push) and `pop()` (Pop from end) on a Python list? Both are $O(1)$ amortized constant time!

practicals.title: Check whether a given number is an Armstrong number and a Palindrome
practicals.aim: Official CBSE Class 10 Practical Program: Write a Python program to check if an input integer is a Palindrome and/or a 3-digit Armstrong number.
algorithm: Read integer n from input().
Palindrome check: compare str(n) with its reverse str(n)[::-1].
Armstrong check: sum each digit raised to the power of total digits and compare with n.
practicals.code:
# CBSE Class 10 Practical: Palindrome & Armstrong Number Checker
num = int(input("Enter a positive integer (e.g. 153 or 121): "))
s = str(num)
power = len(s)

is_palindrome = (s == s[::-1])
armstrong_sum = sum(int(digit) ** power for digit in s)
is_armstrong = (armstrong_sum == num)

print(f"\nNumber Analyzed : {num}")
print(f"Is Palindrome?  : {'✅ Yes' if is_palindrome else '❌ No'} (Reversed: {s[::-1]})")
print(f"Is Armstrong?   : {'✅ Yes' if is_armstrong else '❌ No'} (Digit power sum: {armstrong_sum})")
practicals.vivaTip: 153 is an Armstrong number because $1^3 + 5^3 + 3^3 = 1 + 125 + 27 = 153$. Other 3-digit Armstrong numbers are 370, 371, and 407.

examQuestions.question: Which of the following is an INVALID identifier in Python?
examQuestions.explanation: `None` (with a capital N) is a reserved Python keyword and cannot be used as an identifier. Note that `true` (lowercase) is NOT a keyword (`True` is), so `true` is technically a valid identifier.

examQuestions.question: What will be the output of the following Python expression?
examQuestions.explanation: Step 1: Exponentiation `3 ** 2` = `9`. Step 2: Floor division `16 // 9` = `1` and modulo `4 % 3` = `1`. Step 3: `1 + 1` = `2`.

examQuestions.question: What is the output of `"PYTHON-PROGRAMMING".partition("-")`?
examQuestions.explanation: `.partition(sep)` ALWAYS returns a 3-element tuple `(head, sep, tail)` containing the substring before the separator, the separator itself, and the substring after it.

examQuestions.question: If `f` is a text file object opened in read mode, what is the data type returned by `f.readlines()`?
examQuestions.explanation: `f.readlines()` reads all remaining lines from the file and returns them as a `list` of strings (`list[str]`), whereas `f.read()` and `f.readline()` return a `str`.

examQuestions.question: Which exception is raised by `pickle.load(f)` when it reaches the end of a binary file?
examQuestions.explanation: When `pickle.load(f)` reaches the end of a binary file and no more serialized objects remain, Python raises `EOFError`.

examQuestions.question: Table `STUDENT` has 5 columns and 10 rows. Table `SPORTS` has 3 columns and 6 rows. What will be the Degree and Cardinality of their Cartesian Product (`SELECT * FROM STUDENT, SPORTS`)?
examQuestions.explanation: In a Cartesian Product, Degrees (columns) are ADDED (`5 + 3 = 8`) and Cardinalities (rows) are MULTIPLIED (`10 * 6 = 60`).

examQuestions.question:
Assertion (A): While opening a CSV file for writing in Python on Windows, we pass `newline=""` in the `open()` function.
Reason (R): `newline=""` prevents extra blank lines from being inserted between rows in the CSV file.
options: Both A and R are True and R is the correct explanation for A
Both A and R are True but R is NOT the correct explanation for A
A is True but R is False
A is False but R is True
examQuestions.explanation: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and R directly explains why `newline=""` is passed to `open()` when working with the `csv` module.

examQuestions.question:
Assertion (A): A function definition `def compute(a=10, b, c=20):` is valid in Python.
Reason (R): In a Python function header, default parameters must always appear after non-default positional parameters.
options: Both A and R are True and R is the correct explanation for A
Both A and R are True but R is NOT the correct explanation for A
A is True but R is False
A is False but R is True
examQuestions.explanation: Assertion (A) is False (`def compute(a=10, b, c=20):` raises `SyntaxError: non-default argument follows default argument`), while Reason (R) is True!

examQuestions.question: What is the output of the following Class 10 Python code?
examQuestions.explanation: `L.append([40, 50])` adds the entire list `[40, 50]` as a single nested element at index 3: `[10, 20, 30, [40, 50]]`. Hence `len(L)` is `4`.

examQuestions.question: How many times will the word `"CBSE"` be printed by the following loop?
examQuestions.explanation: `range(10, 2, -3)` generates `10, 7, 4` (stops before `2`). Therefore, the loop runs `3` times.

outputChallenges.prompt: The following code has 4 syntax/runtime errors. Identify the corrected version and test it in the IDE:
outputChallenges.code:
# Broken CBSE Question Snippet:
Def calc_sum(n = 10, m)     # Error 1 & 2
    total = 0
    for i in range(1, m + 1) # Error 3
        if i % 2 = 0:        # Error 4
            total += i
    return total
outputChallenges.runnableCode:
# Corrected Version:
def calc_sum(m, n=10):       # Fix 1: 'def' lowercase, non-default 'm' first, colon ':'
    total = 0
    for i in range(1, m + 1): # Fix 2: Colon ':' at end of for statement
        if i % 2 == 0:        # Fix 3: '==' for equality comparison instead of '='
            total += i
    return total + n

print("Result:", calc_sum(6))
stepByStepTrace: Fix 2: Non-default parameter `m` must come before default parameter `n=10`, and the function header must end with a colon `:`.
Fix 3: The `for` loop header must end with a colon `:`.
Fix 4: Equality comparison inside `if` must use `==` instead of assignment `=`.

vivaCards.question: What is the difference between `r+` and `w+` file modes in Python?
vivaCards.answer: Both `r+` and `w+` allow reading and writing. However, `r+` raises `FileNotFoundError` if the file does not exist and preserves existing content, whereas `w+` creates a new file if it does not exist and overwrites (truncates) existing content immediately!

vivaCards.question: What are Pickling and Unpickling in Python?
vivaCards.answer: **Pickling** (Serialization) is the process of converting a Python object hierarchy (like a list or dict) into a byte stream using `pickle.dump()`. **Unpickling** (Deserialization) is the inverse process of reconstructing the Python object from the byte stream using `pickle.load()`.

vivaCards.question: Why does `stack.append()` and `stack.pop()` represent a LIFO data structure?
vivaCards.answer: Both `.append()` and `.pop()` operate at the same end (the top/tail) of the Python list in $O(1)$ time, ensuring that the **Last** item inserted is the **First** item removed (Last-In, First-Out).

vivaCards.question: Differentiate between `CHAR(n)` and `VARCHAR(n)` in SQL.
vivaCards.answer: `CHAR(n)` is a **fixed-length** string datatype (pads shorter strings with trailing spaces up to length `n`), whereas `VARCHAR(n)` is a **variable-length** string datatype (uses only the exact number of bytes needed for the stored characters).

vivaCards.question: What is the difference between Candidate Key, Primary Key, and Alternate Key?
vivaCards.answer:
- **Candidate Keys**: All attributes capable of uniquely identifying tuples in a table.
- **Primary Key**: The one Candidate Key chosen by the database designer to uniquely identify rows (cannot be `NULL`).
- **Alternate Keys**: Remaining Candidate Keys that were not chosen as the Primary Key ($	ext{Alternate Keys} = 	ext{Candidate Keys} - 	ext{Primary Key}$).

vivaCards.question: What is the difference between `list.pop()` and `list.remove()`?
vivaCards.answer: `list.pop(index)` deletes an element by its **index** and returns the deleted value (defaults to `-1`). `list.remove(value)` deletes the first occurrence of a matching **value** and returns `None`.

fileModes.description: Read only (default). Pointer at start. Raises FileNotFoundError if file does not exist.
Write only. Overwrites (truncates) existing file or creates a new file.
Append only. Pointer at end of file (EOF). Creates new file if missing.
Read & Write. Pointer at start of file. Raises error if file is missing.
Write & Read. Overwrites existing file or creates a new file.
Append & Read. Pointer at EOF for writing; creates file if missing.

sqlRules.rule: COUNT(*) counts all rows including NULLs; COUNT(col) ignores NULL values in that column.
WHERE filters individual rows before GROUP BY; HAVING filters grouped rows after GROUP BY and supports aggregate functions.
Always use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL in WHERE clauses (never use = NULL).
Degree = D1 + D2 (sum of columns); Cardinality = C1 * C2 (product of rows).
CHAR(n) is fixed-length (padded with spaces); VARCHAR(n) is variable-length up to n bytes.
Equi-Join matches columns using '=' (common column appears twice in SELECT *); Natural Join removes the duplicate common column.
